result.reason: Both items describe the core gazlan-witness problem — he cannot testify to his own signature but others can — which is precisely what heading 3 ('Gazlan Witness') introduces, not the son-in-law case under heading 7 where the passage currently sits.

Items 1-4 form a continuous chain discussing the 'prior viewing' (huchzak ktav yado be-veit din) solution and its application to the inheritance/document case (item 1) and the son-in-law case (items 2-4), which matches candidate 0's prose about the same conceptual problem recurring and the same 'prior viewing' response being offered — before the Gemara moves on in candidate 1 to the 'no prior viewing' distinction introduced by Rav Nachman.

All three items directly address the verse 'tachat avotecha yihiyu vanecha' and the claim that it is written as a blessing rather than a legal principle, which is precisely what candidate 2's prose discusses.
The passage is the actual quoted baraita about the house collapse scenario, which the prose in heading 0 ('House Collapse Case') directly introduces and describes.

The passage directly presents the Gemara's challenge that if a grandson cannot claim through his grandfather's right, the ba'al chov could simply say 'yerusha de-avuchon ka shaklis' — exactly the argument described in the 'Baraita Dispute' prose section.

This Gemara passage rejects the idea that a grandson inherits directly from a grandfather, concluding instead that inheritance passes through the father — which is precisely the established premise that leads into the Rav Sheshet query about inheriting through the grave, making it a setup/transition passage that belongs under the 'Rav Sheshet Query' section.
The passage is precisely the dilemma posed to Rav Sheshet about a son inheriting from his mother while in the grave, which is exactly what the 'Rav Sheshet Query' prose describes.

The passage addresses the reinterpretation of the baraita's case involving a father and daughter's son who died in captivity vs. the province with unknown order of death — this is precisely what the 'If Grave Permitted' prose discusses as the Gemara pressing on why the order of death matters, making it a clearly better match than the 'Mother Son House' section.

Both items present the ve-im issa argument — if grave-inheritance were permitted, the order of death would be irrelevant — which is precisely what candidate 1 ('If Grave Permitted') describes in its prose.

The passage contains Abaye's explicit gezerah shavah analogy between 'sibah' for husband and 'sibah' for son — the exact content described in candidate 2's prose, which even quotes the same Aramaic passage verbatim.

The passage describes exactly the Bar Sisan sale case — a seller claiming a field merely called 'of the house of Bar Sisan' is not included in the sale — which is precisely what the 'Bar Sisan Sale' prose section describes.

All five items form one continuous sugya: items 1-3 present the contradictory rulings of Rava and Rav Nachman across the two cases, and items 4-5 resolve those contradictions — exactly the content described in heading 2 ('House Case'), which explicitly covers the contradiction, the house case facts, and the resolution regarding who bears the burden.
